questions.question: Design a search autocomplete/typeahead feature for a 10 million product catalog.
questions.title: Design Search Autocomplete for a Product Catalog
questions.direct_answer: Build a **two-tier system**: a **Redis-backed prefix index** (sorted-set per prefix, sorted by popularity) for sub-10ms suggestions on every keystroke, backed by **Elasticsearch with edge n-gram tokenization** for typo tolerance and richer ranking. **Async pipeline** ingests catalog updates and search-analytics popularity into both stores. Aggressively cache the top N suggestions per prefix at the **CDN/edge** since prefix traffic follows a heavy-tailed distribution (a small set of prefixes dominates).

interviewer_intent.testing: Prefix-search data structures, latency budget per keystroke, ranking by popularity, and cache strategy for a power-law traffic distribution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `LIKE 'query%'` on a relational DB (doesn't scale past 100K products), or treating it as a generic search problem and bolting on Elasticsearch without a prefix index.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Justify the Redis prefix index for the hot path, edge n-gram tokenization in Elasticsearch for the cold path, popularity-weighted ranking with personalization, typo tolerance via Levenshtein at the second tier, and CDN caching for the head of the prefix distribution.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
Autocomplete looks like "prefix lookup," but the operational reality is harder:

- **Latency is brutal** — every keystroke fires a request. Sub-100 ms end-to-end (network + server + render) is the floor; sub-50 ms server-side is what good products hit.
- **Traffic shape is power-law** — the top 1,000 prefixes (`a`, `am`, `ama`, `amaz`, ...) get the vast majority of traffic. Caching the head pays for itself enormously.
- **Catalog is dynamic** — products added, prices changed, items delisted. Stale suggestions hurt revenue (suggest an out-of-stock item, lose the click).
- **Ranking matters more than recall** — the first 5 suggestions are seen 95% of the time. Order by popularity, not alphabet.
- **Typo tolerance** — `"iphn"` should suggest `"iphone"`. Strict prefix matching can't do this; we need Levenshtein/edit-distance.
- **Personalization** — viewing history, location, language affect what should rank where. Adds ~10ms per query.
- **Multi-tenant** — different categories, locales, possibly different sellers each have their own popularity distribution.

The central architectural decision: **a fast hot tier (Redis prefix → sorted suggestions) for the 95% of queries with strict prefix matches, plus a richer cold tier (Elasticsearch with edge n-grams + fuzziness) for typos and complex ranking**, with an async ingestion pipeline keeping both in sync.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- **Suggestion source**: products only, or also queries other users searched?
- **Typo tolerance** required from day 1?
- **Personalization** (recent searches, location, language)?
- **Categories/scoping** (search within "Electronics" only)?
- **Suggestion type**: just strings, or rich (image + price + category)?
- **Number of suggestions returned per request** (typically 5–10)?

**Non-functional**
- **Latency budget** — sub-100 ms end-to-end typical.
- **QPS** — tens of thousands per second for a large product site.
- **Catalog size** — 10M products in this design.
- **Update freshness** — minutes acceptable, or seconds required?
- **Multi-language / multi-region** — separate indices per locale?

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **10M products** in the catalog. Each has a name, ~3 keywords, category, popularity score.
- **Suggestion source**: product names + top-N popular search queries from analytics.
- **30K autocomplete QPS average**, 100K peak. (Each user typing a 5-character query fires ~5 requests.)
- **Typo tolerance** required at the second tier (1–2 character edits).
- **Sub-50 ms p99 server-side**, sub-100 ms end-to-end.
- **Updates within 5 minutes** of catalog changes.
- **Top 10 suggestions returned per request**.
- **Multi-locale** (en, es, fr, etc.) with separate index per locale.
- **Personalization is optional** — layer added later, doesn't gate v1.
- **CDN-cacheable for the top 10K prefixes** with 60-second TTL.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- 30K QPS average, 100K peak across all locales.
- Per locale (assume en is 60%): 60K QPS peak on the en-index.
- A single Redis node handles ~80K simple GETs/sec; sharded Redis cluster easily.

**Storage**

- Prefix index in Redis: 10M products × average 12 chars × (1 + 2 + ... + 12) prefixes per product = ~80M unique prefixes per locale.
- Each prefix → sorted set of top 10 suggestions × ~50 bytes per entry = ~500 bytes per prefix entry → **~40 GB Redis per locale** (compact format).
- Elasticsearch index: 10M products × ~2 KB per document = **~20 GB per locale**, replicated to ~60 GB.
- Total across 5 locales: ~200 GB Redis, ~300 GB ES. Well within a small production cluster.

**CDN cache hit rate**

- Top 10K prefixes drive ~80% of traffic (power-law).
- 60-second TTL at CDN → ~80% of QPS never reaches origin.
- Origin sees only ~20K QPS at peak — trivially handled.

**Latency budget breakdown** (server-side, p99)

- Network ingress + auth: 5 ms
- Redis prefix lookup: 5 ms
- Optional ES query (typo path): 20 ms
- Personalization re-rank: 5 ms
- Hydration (image, price): 10 ms
- Total: ~45 ms (Redis-only path); ~65 ms (with ES fallback).

**Conclusion**: hot path is Redis-only at <30ms; ES is the typo/long-tail safety net. CDN absorbs 80% of traffic before it reaches us.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
Single endpoint, designed for CDN cacheability:

```http
GET /api/v1/autocomplete?q=ama&locale=en&limit=10

200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=120

{
  "query": "ama",
  "suggestions": [
    {
      "text": "amazon basics",
      "type": "product",
      "product_id": "p_8712",
      "image_url": "https://cdn/.../amazon-basics.jpg",
      "category": "Office",
      "score": 0.94,
      "highlight_ranges": [[0,3]]
    },
    {
      "text": "amalfi lemons",
      "type": "product",
      "product_id": "p_4421",
      ...
    }
  ],
  "trace_id": "abc-123"
}
```

**Key design choices in the contract:**

- **`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`** — lets CDN and browser cache aggressively. The 60-second window is the freshness vs hit-rate trade-off.
- **`stale-while-revalidate`** — CDN serves stale while async-fetching fresh in background. Eliminates user-visible cache misses.
- **`highlight_ranges`** — lets the client UI bold the matched portion without doing its own substring search.
- **No POST body** — GET with query string so CDN can key on the URL.

**Personalization opt-in:**

```http
GET /api/v1/autocomplete?q=ama&locale=en&user_id=u_99
Cache-Control: private, max-age=10
```

When user_id is present, response is `private` and short-TTL — not CDN-cacheable across users.

High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
Two paths: **read** (the hot keystroke loop) and **ingest** (catalog and analytics updates). ```mermaid flowchart TB User([User Browser]) CDN[CDN

source of truth] Analytics[(Search Analytics
clicks, impressions)] Kafka{{Kafka
catalog.changed
search.event}} Indexer[Index Builder
prefix expansion] Popularity[Popularity Pipeline
spark/flink job] User -->|keystroke| CDN CDN -.miss.-> LB LB --> AC AC --> Redis AC -.typo path.-> ES AC -.opt-in.-> Personalization Catalog -->|CDC| Kafka Analytics -->|stream| Kafka Kafka --> Indexer Kafka --> Popularity Popularity --> Indexer Indexer --> Redis Indexer --> ES classDef edge fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef bus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b class CDN,LB edge class AC,Indexer,Popularity,Personalization svc class Redis,ES,Catalog,Analytics store class Kafka bus ``` **Read path:** browser → CDN → (on miss) Autocomplete Service → Redis prefix ZSET → hydrate top 10 → return. ES only consulted when prefix lookup yields fewer than threshold (e.g., < 3) or the query has unusual character patterns suggesting a typo. **Ingest path:** Catalog CDC + search-event stream → Kafka → (1) Index Builder expands prefixes and writes to Redis + ES; (2) Popularity Pipeline aggregates clicks/conversions over rolling windows and publishes scores back into the indexer.

sections.title: Read-Path Algorithm
LLD — Class Design of the Autocomplete Service
Ingestion Pipeline — Keeping Indices Fresh
sections.content:
**Sources of change**:

1. **Catalog CDC** (Debezium on PostgreSQL) — product added/updated/deleted/restocked.
2. **Search analytics stream** — every search and click event flows to Kafka.

**Index Builder** consumes both:

- **On catalog change**: tokenize the product name, expand each token to prefixes, upsert into Redis and Elasticsearch. Latency: catalog change visible in autocomplete within ~5 minutes.
- **On out-of-stock event**: remove product from prefix indices (or mark with low score so it ranks last). Stale stock is one of the highest-impact bugs.

**Popularity pipeline** (Spark/Flink job, runs every 15 minutes):

- Aggregates clicks, conversions, and impressions over a 7-day window with exponential time decay.
- Computes per-product popularity scores.
- Emits updated scores to Kafka → Index Builder updates ZSET scores.

**Trim policy**:

- Each prefix ZSET keeps the top 10 entries; less popular products fall off naturally.
- Trimming on every upsert (`ZREMRANGEBYRANK key 0 -11`) is cheap.

**Cold start for a new product**:

- New product gets a default popularity score (e.g., based on category average).
- After ~24 hours of impressions, real popularity replaces the default.

sections.title: Storage Choice and Sharding
sections.content:
**Why Redis for the hot tier**

- Sorted sets are exactly the right primitive: O(log n) insertion, O(log n + N) range read, intrinsic ordering by score.
- In-memory latency is what makes the 5ms Redis budget achievable.
- Cluster mode shards by key (`ac:en:ama` hashes to a specific shard) — horizontal scaling is built-in.
- TTL not needed for prefixes (managed by upsert/trim).

**Sharding** — hash-based on the full prefix key. Hot prefixes (`a`, `am`, ...) end up on different shards; the head of the distribution distributes naturally.

**Why Elasticsearch for the cold tier**

- Edge n-gram tokenization handles prefix queries efficiently.
- Built-in `fuzziness` parameter handles typos.
- Rich relevance scoring (BM25 + custom function scores).
- Clusters on standard infrastructure; well-understood operations.

**Why not put everything in ES?**

- ES query latency is consistently in the 10–20ms range; Redis is 1–2ms. For a per-keystroke API, the difference is huge.
- ES is a heavier component to scale to 100K QPS; Redis at the front absorbs the bulk.

**Why not put everything in Redis?**

- Typo tolerance and rich text scoring aren't Redis primitives.
- Storing rich product documents (name + description + attributes) for fuzzy match would explode Redis memory.

sections.title: Caching, Hot Prefixes, and CDN Strategy
sections.content:
**CDN cache (the biggest win)**:

- `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=120` on every anonymous response.
- Top 10K prefixes drive ~80% of traffic → CDN absorbs ~80% of QPS.
- Origin sees ~20K QPS at peak instead of 100K — fifth of the load.
- 60-second TTL is the freshness/hit-rate trade-off; product team can tune.

**In-process Caffeine cache** on each Autocomplete Service instance:

- Cache `(locale, prefix) → hydrated suggestions` for 30 seconds.
- Per-instance hit rate ~70% on top prefixes.
- Eliminates Redis hops for the head of the distribution.

**Hot-prefix problem**:

- Even with CDN, certain prefixes (`a`, `e`, `i`, ...) get extreme traffic.
- Solution: replicate hot keys across multiple Redis shards (`ac:en:a:0`, `ac:en:a:1`, ...) and pick randomly on read.
- Triggered when a prefix's per-second QPS exceeds threshold (instrumented separately).

**Negative caching**:

- Empty prefix results cached for 60 seconds.
- Prevents typo-driven prefix bombing from hammering ES.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Redis cluster outage**

- Autocomplete Service falls back to Elasticsearch directly.
- Latency spikes from ~30ms to ~50ms; service stays up.
- CDN keeps serving cached responses for the long tail of TTLs.
- Per-instance Caffeine cache absorbs popular queries while Redis recovers.

**Elasticsearch outage**

- Typo-tolerance feature degrades — only strict prefix matches return.
- Service stays functional for ~95% of queries (where strict prefix is enough).
- Alerting fires; operator manually disables fuzzy fallback to skip slow ES probe.

**Index Builder lag**

- New products take longer than 5 minutes to appear in suggestions.
- Catalog stays the source of truth; no data loss.
- Alert on Kafka consumer lag > 10 minutes.

**Stale out-of-stock items**

- Real-world high-impact bug: suggesting an out-of-stock product wastes a click.
- Real-time stock event stream bypasses the popularity pipeline; updates within seconds.
- Hydration step also filters: if `product.in_stock = false` at hydration time, demote/skip.

**CDN cache poisoning**

- A malformed query that returns garbage gets cached and amplified.
- Mitigation: input sanitization rejects requests with disallowed chars before they reach origin.
- Anomaly detection on response sizes; auto-purge suspicious cache entries.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `autocomplete.latency` (p50/p95/p99) — SLO p99 < 50ms server-side.
- `autocomplete.cache.hit_rate{layer=cdn|caffeine|redis}` — stratified.
- `autocomplete.fuzzy_path_rate` — % of requests that hit ES.
- `redis.shard.qps` — detect hot prefixes.
- `index_builder.lag_seconds` — freshness alert.
- `popularity.pipeline.last_update_age` — ranking-model freshness alert.

**Logging**

- Sample 1% of full request/response for query analytics.
- Never log user_id with query in same row (privacy).

**Security**

- **Rate limit per IP** at CDN edge (1,000 RPS per IP) — prevents prefix-bomb attacks.
- **Input validation** — max 50 chars, ASCII or locale charset, reject SQL-injection patterns.
- **No auth required** for the public autocomplete; personalization endpoint requires auth token.
- **Anonymized search analytics** — query data flows to analytics without user_id; personalization features computed in a separate trusted pipeline.
- **PII filter** — reject suggestions matching credit-card / SSN patterns even if they occur in product names (rare but possible).

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (300K QPS, 100M products):**

- **Embed the prefix index** in each Autocomplete Service instance using a memory-mapped trie (e.g., FST). Eliminates the Redis hop entirely; trade memory per instance for latency.
- **Per-region index replicas** — Redis Cluster + ES per geographic region; client routed to nearest.
- **GPU-accelerated re-ranking** — deep learning models for personalization at sub-10ms latency.
- **Vector search for semantic suggestions** — "red shoe" matches "crimson sneaker" via embedding similarity.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **CDN TTL** — 60 seconds is conservative. Going to 5 minutes would shed origin load further but at the cost of stale stock visibility.
- **Trie vs ZSET in Redis** — a trie via Redis modules (RedisGears or RediSearch) might be slightly more memory-efficient at high cardinality but adds operational complexity.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **`LIKE 'q%'` on PostgreSQL** — doesn't scale past ~100K rows for autocomplete latency.
- **Trie in application memory only** — every restart re-loads from source; horizontal scale-out hard. (Future enhancement, not v1.)
- **Single ES-only design** — ES p99 is too high for per-keystroke without front-cache.
- **Real-time popularity** — popularity is a smoothed signal; sub-minute updates add cost without UX gain.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two-tier architecture** — Redis prefix ZSETs for the strict-match hot path (95% of queries, sub-10ms), Elasticsearch with edge n-grams for typo tolerance.
- **One ZSET per `(locale, prefix)`** sorted by popularity, capped at top 10 — read is one Redis call, write is upsert + trim.
- **CDN cache with 60s TTL** absorbs ~80% of traffic; origin sees a fraction.
- **In-process Caffeine cache** on each service instance gives an extra layer for hot prefixes.
- **Async ingestion pipeline** — catalog CDC + analytics stream feed an Index Builder; popularity pipeline updates scores every 15 minutes.
- **Real-time stock filter at hydration** — the highest-impact failure (suggesting out-of-stock) handled outside the popularity loop.
- **Personalization is opt-in** — anonymous calls are CDN-cacheable; logged-in calls bypass CDN.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Suggestion source — product names only or also popular search queries from other users?
- Typo tolerance from day one?
- Personalization (recent searches, location)?
- Multi-locale or single?
- Rich suggestions (image + price) or just text?

**Assumptions for this design**

10 million products, multi-locale, 30K autocomplete QPS average / 100K peak, sub-50ms p99 server-side, sub-100ms end-to-end. Updates within 5 minutes of catalog changes. Top 10 suggestions returned. Personalization optional.

**Quick capacity check**

- 100K peak QPS, but power-law distribution means top 10K prefixes drive ~80% of traffic
- CDN with 60s TTL absorbs that 80% — origin sees ~20K QPS
- Redis storage: ~80M unique prefixes per locale at ~500 bytes each = ~40 GB Redis per locale
- Latency budget: Redis 5ms + optional ES 20ms + hydration 10ms + personalization 5ms = under 50ms

**The central architectural decision — two-tier index**

- Hot tier: Redis sorted set per `(locale, prefix)`, members are product IDs, scores are popularity — one ZREVRANGE call returns top 10
- Cold tier: Elasticsearch with edge n-gram tokenizer for typo tolerance and richer ranking
- Most queries are served from Redis only; ES kicks in when prefix yields <3 results or query looks like a typo

**Why one ZSET per prefix, not a trie**

- Trie in Redis would mean multiple node fetches per query — latency killer
- Sorted set lookup is one call, O(log n)
- Cost is storage duplication (each suggestion appears under each of its prefixes), which is acceptable

**Why edge n-gram in Elasticsearch**

- Indexes every prefix of every token at write time, so prefix queries become term lookups
- Gives us typo tolerance via fuzziness parameter
- Index is larger but query latency is consistent in the 10-20ms range

**High-level shape**

- Read: browser → CDN → (on miss) Autocomplete Service → Redis prefix ZSET → hydrate top 10 → return
- Read with typo: same path, but if Redis has fewer than 3 results, also query ES, merge, dedupe
- Ingest: Catalog CDC + search-event stream → Kafka → Index Builder expands prefixes and writes to both Redis and ES
- Popularity pipeline: Spark/Flink job runs every 15 minutes, computes scores from clicks/conversions with time decay, updates ZSET scores

**Read algorithm step by step**

1. Redis: `ZREVRANGE ac:{locale}:{prefix} 0 9 WITHSCORES`
2. If results <3 or typo heuristic: ES `match` query with `fuzziness: AUTO`, merge
3. If user_id present: personalization re-rank
4. Hydrate: pipelined Redis HGETs for product metadata
5. Return

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `PrefixIndex` interface (RedisPrefixIndex impl; could swap for in-memory FST)
- `FuzzyIndex` interface (Elasticsearch impl; could swap for vector search)
- `TypoDetector` decides whether to consult fuzzy index
- `PersonalizationRanker` is its own collaborator, absent for anonymous calls
- `IndexBuilder` and `PrefixExpander` handle the write side

**Caching layers**

- CDN: 60s TTL with `stale-while-revalidate` — absorbs ~80% of QPS
- In-process Caffeine on each service instance — 30s TTL on hydrated suggestions
- Hot-prefix sharding: replicate top prefixes across multiple Redis keys, pick randomly
- Negative caching for empty results to defend against prefix bombing

**Ingestion pipeline**

- Catalog CDC via Debezium on PostgreSQL → Kafka
- Search analytics stream → Kafka
- Index Builder consumes both, tokenizes and expands prefixes, upserts into Redis + ES, trims ZSETs to top 10
- Popularity pipeline runs every 15 minutes — popularity is a smoothed signal, sub-minute updates aren't worth the cost
- Real-time stock events bypass popularity — out-of-stock filter at hydration

**Failure handling**

- Redis down: fall back to ES directly; latency rises from 30ms to 50ms but service stays up
- ES down: typo path degraded, strict prefix still works for ~95% of queries
- Index Builder lag: catalog still source of truth; alert on >10 min lag
- Out-of-stock bug: hydration filters in real time; doesn't depend on popularity pipeline
- CDN cache poisoning: input sanitization rejects malformed queries before reaching origin

**Production extras**

- Rate limit per IP at CDN edge (1000 RPS) to prevent prefix-bomb attacks
- Input validation: max 50 chars, locale charset only
- Anonymized analytics for non-personalization features
- PII filter on suggestion strings
- Distributed tracing across CDN → service → Redis/ES

**At 10× scale**

- Embedded memory-mapped trie (FST) per service instance — eliminates Redis hop
- Per-region indices for geo-proximity
- GPU-accelerated personalization re-ranking
- Vector search for semantic suggestions ("red shoe" → "crimson sneaker")

**Recommendation**

**Two-tier index — Redis prefix ZSETs for the hot strict-match path, Elasticsearch with edge n-grams for typo tolerance — fronted by a CDN with 60-second TTL on anonymous responses, an async ingestion pipeline keeping both in sync, and real-time stock filtering at hydration to avoid suggesting out-of-stock products** — the same architecture Amazon, Etsy, and Shopify run for catalog autocomplete.

How does your design change if the same query needs to scope to a category (e.g., autocomplete within "Electronics" only)?
Walk through how out-of-stock items are removed from suggestions in under 30 seconds.
How would you A/B-test a new ranking algorithm without regressing latency or violating the 60s CDN TTL?
